'''''Logfia minima''''', '''small cudweed''', is a plant in the [[Asteraceae|daisy family]] which grows on bare ground and in acid grassland. It is native to Europe and parts of north Africa, and it has been introduced to North America.

==Description==
Small cudweed is a small annual plant, growing up to about 10 or 20 cm tall, with a slender, usually upright but sometimes prostrate stem that may be branched towards the top on more vigorous specimens. The whole plant is usually grey-green with a fluffy indumentum of short, simple hairs. The leaves are alternate, narrowly oval with a pointed tip, up to about 10 mm long, and generally held closely pressed up to the stem or branch.
[[File:Filago minima kz09.jpg|thumb|The overwintering seedlings have a distinctive greenish-white colour.]]

The flowerheads occur in groups of 3-7 at the tips of the stem and branches, or in the forks of the branches. They are not overtopped by the leaves, as they are in some other members of this genus. Each capitulum is about 2 mm in diameter and like a 5-sided pyramid when young, opening out into a star shape as they mature. There are many small involucral bracts around the capitulum, in several irregular rows, each bract being up to 3 mm long and narrowly lanceolate. The numerous tiny flowers are tubular, yellow, about 2.5 mm long and 5-lobed at the tip. The outer ones are female and the inner ones bisexual. All the flowers contain five stamens and one pistil.
[[File:Filago minima sl13.jpg|thumb|Fruiting flowerheads]]

The fruits are [[achene]]s of two types: the outer ones smooth, about 1 mm long and enclosed by the papery involucral bracts; the inner ones about half that length, papillose, and with a pappus of short white hairs at the end. Pollination and dispersal are by wind, as is common in the [[Asteraceae|daisy family]].<ref name=Sell2006>{{cite book |last1=Sell |first1=Peter |last2=Murrell |first2=Gina |title=Flora of Great Britain and Ireland, vol. 4 ''Campanulaceae'' - ''Asteraceae'' |year=2006 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge}}</ref><ref name=Stace2019>{{Cite book |last=Stace |first=C.A. |title=New Flora of the British Isles |publisher=C & M Floristics |year=2019 |isbn=978-1-5272-2630-2 |edition=4th |location=Middlewood Green}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
There are many small species of cudweed, found in both the [[Old World|Old]] and the [[New World]], and they can be difficult to identify and classify, owing to their size and the simplification of their features. The two genera ''Gnaphalium'' and ''Filago'' have existed since pre-Linnean times, and species have often been assigned to one or the other of these genera by different authors. Small cudweed may, for example, have been described as ''Gnaphalium minimum'' by [[Matthias de l'Obel|Lobelius]] and [[Johann Bauhin|Bauhin]], but any name they used is pre-Linnean and so does not stand according to the rules of [[botanical nomenclature]]. [[Carl Linnaeus|Linnaeus]] did not include small cudweed in his ''[[Species Plantarum]]'', although he does mention the ''Gnaphalium minimum'' of the earlier authors, as a synonym of ''Filago montana'',<ref>{{Cite book |last=Linnaeus |first=Carl |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/31274#page/906/mode/1up |title=Species Plantarum |year=1753 |page=872}}</ref> which in turn is now thought to have been confused with ''[[Filago arvensis]]''.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Filago arvensis L. {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:207840-1 |access-date=2026-04-01 |website=Plants of the World Online |language=en}}</ref>

The modern species of small cudweed was therefore first named ''Gnaphalium minimum'' by [[James Edward Smith (botanist)|J.E. Smith]] in his ''Flora Britannica'' of 1800.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Smith |first=Jacobo Eduardo |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/29423#page/445/mode/1up |title=Flora Britannica |publisher=J. White |year=1800 |volume=2 |location=Fleet Street |pages=873–4}}</ref> This is the first valid name for the plant which, as the current name is different, makes it the [[basionym]]. He also gave it a descriptive name in the pre-Linnean style: ''Gnaphalium caule erecto ramoso, foliis lanceolatis acutis planis, floribus conicis subconcertis lateralibus terminalibusque'', which can be translated as "the cudweed with an erect, branched stem, flat, pointed, lanceolate leaves and conical, closely clustered lateral and terminal flowers".<ref name=gbif>{{Cite web |title=Logfia minima (Sm.) Dumort. |url=https://www.gbif.org/species/3088922 |access-date=2026-03-30 |website=www.gbif.org |language=en}}</ref>

A few years later, in 1807, [[Christiaan Hendrik Persoon|Persoon]] reassigned it to the genus ''Filago'', as ''F. minima''.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Filago minima (Sm.) Pers. {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:207920-1 |access-date=2026-04-01 |website=Plants of the World Online |language=en}}</ref> This name has generally been used ever since,<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Clapham |first1=A.R. |title=Flora of the British Isles |last2=Tutin |first2=T. |last3=Warburg |first3=E.F. |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=1952}}</ref><ref name="Sell2006" /> although there is a competing school of thought.

The genus ''Logfia'' (along with ''Oglifa'', ''Gifola'' and ''Ifloga'') was created by the French botanist [[Henri Cassini]] in 1819 by splitting the large genus ''Filago'' into  five separate but extremely similar genera, and he acknowledged the pedantry of his classification by using anagrams of the word "Filago" for some of the new taxa. The morphological difference between Cassini's ''Filago'' and ''Logfia'' is largely based on minute differences in the shape of the [[Phyllary|phyllaries]] around the capitulum,<ref name="Stace2019" /> but [[Barthélemy Charles Joseph Dumortier|Dumortier]] was evidently convinced enough to assign small cudweed to the new genus in his ''Florula Belgica'' of 1827 (p. 68).<ref>{{Cite book |last=Dumortier |first=B.C. |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/328648#page/78/mode/1up |title=Florula Belgica |year=1827 |location=Tournai |page=68}}</ref> However, this name was not commonly used until recently, when DNA analysis in 2010 showed how the numerous ''Filago'' species are related,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Galbany-Casals |first1=Mercè |last2=Andrés-Sánchez |first2=Santiago |last3=Garcia-Jacas |first3=Núria |last4=Susanna |first4=Alfonso |last5=Rico |first5=Enrique |last6=Martínez-Ortega |first6=M. Montserrat |year=2010 |title=How many of Cassini anagrams should there be? Molecular systematics and phylogenetic relationships in the Filago group (Asteraceae, Gnaphalieae), with special focus on the genus Filago |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/tax.596003 |journal=Taxon |language=en |volume=59 |issue=6 |pages=1671–1689 |doi=10.1002/tax.596003 |bibcode=2010Taxon..59.1671G |issn=0040-0262|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and Cassini/Dumortier's name was revived in 2013.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Taxonomic revision of the genus Logfia (Asteraceae, Gnaphalieae) in the Mediterranean region |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/253952056 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230712074828/https://www.researchgate.net/publication/253952056_Taxonomic_revision_of_the_genus_Logfia_Asteraceae_Gnaphalieae_in_the_Mediterranean_region |archive-date=2023-07-12 |access-date=2026-03-31 |website=ResearchGate |language=en}}</ref> The correct scientific name for this plant is therefore now ''Logfia minima'' (Sm.) Dumort., but older books refer to it as ''Filago minima'' (Sm.) Pers.. It is almost impossible to key out these two genera in the field.<ref name=Stace2019 /><ref name=Rich1998>{{cite book |last1=Rich |first1=T.C.G. |last2=Jermy |first2=A.C. |title=Plant Crib 1998 |year=1998 |publisher=Botanical Society of the British Isles |location=London |isbn=0-901-158-28-3}}</ref>

Its chromosome number is 2''n'' = 28.<ref name=Stace2019 />

There are no known hybrids and it has no currently accepted subspecies.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Stace |first1=C.A. |title=Hybridization and the Flora of the British Isles |date=1975 |publisher=Academic Press |location=London |isbn=0-12-661650-7}}</ref><ref name="powo" />

The common name "cudweed" was first used by William Turner in 1548 and is thought to be a contraction of "cottonweed", as all cudweeds are covered with downy, white hairs.<ref>{{Citation |title=cudweed |date=2025-12-24 |work=Wiktionary, the free dictionary |url=https://en.wiktionary.org/w/index.php?title=cudweed&oldid=88715416 |access-date=2026-04-01 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Cudweed |url=https://www.oed.com/dictionary/cudweed_n?tl=true |access-date=1 April 2026 |website=Oxford English Dictionary}}</ref> Its name in French is ''cotonnière naine'' (dwarf cottonweed).<ref name=Guillemot2023>{{Cite book |last=Guillemot |first=Vincent |title=Flore du Massif armoricain et ses marges |publisher=Editions Biotope |year=2023 |isbn=978-2-36662-301-7 |location=Mèze |language=fr}}</ref>

==Distribution and status==
Small cudweed is native to Europe and North Africa, possibly just extending into western Asia. It has occasionlly been introduced to the United States since 1878 as a weed associated with shipping and transport, but it does not persist except in the pacific north-west, around [[Washington (state)|Washington State]] and [[British Columbia]], where it has been seen often in recent years.<ref name=powo>{{Cite web |title=Logfia minima (Sm.) Dumort. {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:231067-1 |access-date=2026-03-28 |website=Plants of the World Online |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Logfia minima in Flora of North America @ efloras.org |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=250067122 |access-date=2026-04-02 |website=www.efloras.org}}</ref><ref name="gbif" />

In Britain it grows from nearly sea level up to about 475 m, reaching its altitudinal limit on [[Titterstone Clee Hill|Titterstone Clee]] in Shropshire.<ref name= "Lockton2015" /><ref>{{cite web |last1=Pearman |first1=D.A. |title=Altitudinal Limits of British Plants, 2021 |url=https://bsbi.org/take-part/projects/altitudes}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=PlantAtlas |url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.7mm340 |access-date=2026-03-29 |website=plantatlas2020.org}}</ref> It is widespread and possibly increasing, so it is classified as LC ([[Least-concern species|least concern]]), but there are places where it has declined considerably in the last hundred years or so. A recent review of England redesignated it as NT ([[Near-threatened species|near threatened]]).

There is no global assessment of small cudweed, and in Europe it has been studied very little, so its status is unknown.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Logfia minima - (Sm.) Dumort. |url=https://eunis.eea.europa.eu/species/161400 |access-date=2026-04-02 |website=eunis.eea.europa.eu}}</ref>

It is considered an [[axiophyte]] in most British counties, which means that it mainly grows in places that are of high conservation value.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Axiophytes |url=https://bsbi.org/learn/getting-started/terms/general-terms/axiophytes |access-date=2026-03-29 |website=bsbi.org |language=en}}</ref>

==Habitat and ecology==
The main habitat of small cudweed is in acid grassland, particularly [[British NVC community U1|U1 ''Festuca ovina'']] grassland on sandy or rocky substrates in Britain.<ref name=Rodwell1992>{{cite book |last=Rodwell |first=J.S. |title=British Plant Communities, vol. 3: Grasslands and montane communities|year=1992 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge |isbn=0-521-39166-0}}</ref><ref name=Lockton2015>{{cite book |last1=Lockton |first1=Alex |last2=Whild |first2=Sarah |title=The Flora and Vegetation of Shropshire |date=2015 |publisher=Shropshire Botanical Society |location=Montford Bridge |url=https://archive.org/details/flora-and-vegetation-of-shropshire-2015|isbn=978-0-9530937-2-4}}</ref><ref name=Crawley2005>{{cite book |last1=Crawley |first1=M.J. |title=The Flora of Berkshire |date=2005 |publisher=Brambleby Books |location=Harpenden |isbn=0-9543347-4-4}}</ref> Its [[Indicator value|Ellenberg-type indicator values]] in Britain are L = 8, F = 3, R = 4, N = 2 and S = 0, which reflects how it grows in full sunlight on dry, acid soils with very low nutrient levels and no salt. In Europe, the recently recalibrated scores are L = 9, F = 3, R = 4, N = 1, S = 0 and T = 6, which suggests that it prefers even brighter conditions and even lower nutrients.<ref name="Plantatt">{{cite web |last1=Hill |first1=M.O. |last2=Preston |first2=C.D. |last3=Roy |first3=D.B. |title=PLANTATT - Attributes of British and Irish Plants - Spreadsheet |url=https://www.brc.ac.uk/biblio/plantatt-attributes-british-and-irish-plants-spreadsheet |publisher=UK Biological Records Centre}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Tichý |first1=Lubomír |last2=Axmanová |first2=Irena |last3=Dengler |first3=Jürgen |last4=Guarino |first4=Riccardo |last5=Jansen |first5=Florian |last6=Midolo |first6=Gabriele |last7=Nobis |first7=Michael P. |last8=Van Meerbeek |first8=Koenraad |last9=Aćić |first9=Svetlana |last10=Attorre |first10=Fabio |last11=Bergmeier |first11=Erwin |last12=Biurrun |first12=Idoia |last13=Bonari |first13=Gianmaria |last14=Bruelheide |first14=Helge |last15=Campos |first15=Juan Antonio |year=2023 |title=Ellenberg-type indicator values for European vascular plant species |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/jvs.13168 |journal=Journal of Vegetation Science |volume=34 |issue=1 |article-number=e13168 |doi=10.1111/jvs.13168 |bibcode=2023JVegS..34E3168T |hdl=11585/918013 |issn=1100-9233|hdl-access=free }}</ref>

A few pests and parasites have been recorded on small cudweed:
* the beetle ''[[Olibrus pygmaeus]]'' feeds on the flowers;
* the weevil ''Acentrotypus brunnipes'' produces galls on the stems;
* the [[Heteroptera|bug]] ''Microplax interrupta'' feeds on the flowers;
* the fungus-like [[Chromista|chromist]] ''Pustula obtusata'' forms patches on the leaves;
* and, in North America, the larvae of the [[American lady]] butterfly feed on this plant.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Filago minima – Plant Parasites of Europe |url=https://bladmineerders.nl/en/host-plants/plantae/spermatopsida/angiosperma/eudicots/superasterids/asterids/campanulids/asterales/asteraceae/asteroideae/gnaphalieae/filago/filago-minima/ |access-date=2026-04-06 |website=bladmineerders.nl}}</ref>
